KEY MESSAGE 1...A cold front will sink south through the region
this evening yielding cooler weather for Thursday.

Low pressure tracking across northern New England will move 
into Nova Scotia tonight. Associated with this low is a frontal 
boundary that extends southwest into the Ohio Valley. This front
will continue to slide south across the region this afternoon 
and into this evening. After a round of showers and some rumbles
of thunder earlier today, temperatures have been knocked down 
into the 70s for many areas. Some recovery is possible for the 
rest of the afternoon with highs still forecast to top out in 
the low 80s for these areas. Elsewhere, temperatures have 
remained well into mid to upper 80s under mostly sunny skies. 
Some showers remain possible in southern areas through the early
evening hours before diminishing.

After the front passes by this evening, cooler air will briefly
return overnight tonight into Thursday. With skies clearing 
across northern areas overnight, lows in the 50s are expected 
for most areas, with 40s in the higher elevations. For southern 
areas, more in the way of cloud cover is expected to persist, 
which will keep overnight lows mostly in the 60s. For Thursday, 
much of the day is expected to be dry with a mix of sun and 
clouds. However, the front will begin to slowly work its way 
back north late in the day, so cannot rule out a few showers 
across the Delmarva as a result. Highs will be generally uniform
in the low to mid 60s with onshore flow. 


KEY MESSAGE 2...A strong cold front passage Friday evening will
bring windy conditions, showers and potential for some 
thunderstorms, and colder temperatures into the weekend.

A sharp upper-level trough is forecast to arrive across the 
East Coast on Friday, then gradually lift out over the weekend. 
This will drive rapidly strengthening surface low pressure just 
north of our area Friday, with an associated strong cold front 
sweeping through. A consensus of guidance has slowed the passage
of the front later in the day, most likely during the evening
hours (4-8 PM), likely moving from our western most zones and 
offshore within about 3 hours or so.

A warm and increasingly moist airmass ahead of this system will
provide modest instability and decent boundary layer mixing as 
the strong cold front approaches on Friday. Large scale forcing 
for ascent will increase with the arrival of the robust upper- 
level trough and cold front. It appears there will be a round of
showers and a few thunderstorms overnight Thursday night into 
early Friday morning associated with the warm advection surge
aloft. There should then be a break in convection by midday
prior to the cold front's arrival late in the day and into the
evening. A line or broken line of showers and storms should
develop along or just ahead of the front. Cannot rule out some 
severe thunderstorm potential, especially if any more robust 
convection can materialize along the cold front.

While it will be mostly cloudy, strong warm advection will 
boost temperatures up well into the 70s and low 80s ahead of the
front. As surface pressure falls rapidly amid a strengthening 
southwesterly gradient, breezy conditions will likely develop 
outside of any showers and storms with gusts of 20-30 mph 
possible.

During and after cold frontal passage, strong cold air 
advection will occur as the sharp trough aloft sweeps through.
However, the timing of this now looks to trail behind the front
until sometime after midnight. This will support efficient 
mixing of winds aloft down toward the surface in the form of 
frequent wind gusts as temperatures plummet into the 50s then 
40s overnight. Boundary layer winds could be as high as 40-50 
mph for a few hours in the wake of the front, which could 
warrant a Wind Advisory. However, the threat of winds of this
magnitude have lessened some given the later timing of the
system. The timing of the peak winds now appears to be focused 
during the overnight hours and into Saturday morning, with gusts
of 30-40 mph likely.

The coldest airmass so far this season will settle into the 
area Saturday into Saturday night. High temperatures Saturday 
are only in the low to mid 50s in most areas (40s north of 
I-78). Breezy conditions will continue, with northwest winds 
gusting 30-40 mph possible in the morning before gradually 
diminishing later in the day.


KEY MESSAGE 3...Widespread frost and freeze conditions are 
increasingly likely Saturday night.

As strong surface high pressure settles nearly overhead into 
Saturday night, temperatures will cool significantly with 
radiational cooling. This should result in widespread low 
temperatures in the 30s Saturday night into Sunday morning, and
